title: Per-request economics: hypothesis & proof plan
body:
Purpose:
Short working brief to turn the abstract claim "we're materially faster and cheaper per request" into a set of testable hypotheses, customer-facing proof points, and a prioritized experiment playbook. This is intentionally tactical — goal is to produce 2–3 bite-sized artifacts reps can use in field demos and 1 reproducible lab benchmark for engineering to own.

Audience: sales reps (mid-market / enterprise AE), solutions engineers, product marketing, applied benchmarks team.

High-level messaging angles (pick 1–2 per account):
- Speed-first: "We deliver predictable p95s so interactive features feel instant — fewer user retries, higher conversion."
- Cost-first: "Lower average token cost and session amortization means same feature for less spend — or richer features for same spend."
- Resilience-as-economics: "Graceful fallback and model routing reduce expensive outages and emergency overprovisioning."

Core hypotheses (testable statements):
H1 — Micro-latency delta: For typical 128–512 token agent queries, Redwood median/per-request latency is >=30% lower than Competitor A on the same regional GPU class.
H2 — Token unit cost: For steady-state QPS workloads (1–10k qps per cluster), Redwood per-token compute cost (normalized) is 15–40% lower because of batching + KV caching effects.
H3 — Session amortization: For multi-turn sessions (10+ turns, 100–1000 tokens total), Redwood effective cost per user session is 20–50% lower due to prefix caching and routing to smaller variants.
H4 — Tail avoidance: Under microburst traffic, Redwood's p99 tail increases less than Competitor B because of adaptive batching & routing.

Minimum proof matrix (what we need to show):
- Synthetic bench: p50/p95/p99 latencies for 3 payload sizes (short: 32 tokens, med: 256, long: 1024) under controlled QPS (1, 50, 500) across 3 model families (base-small, base-medium, chat-xxl) and same GPU type. Include cold vs warm (KV cache primed) runs.
- Cost model: run same scenario with cost annotations: GPU-hours used, inferred compute seconds, token counts; convert to normalized $/1k tokens using published instance pricing. Show caching/batching delta explicitly.
- Session sim: synthetic user session generator to mimic real UX patterns (think chat, autocomplete, summarization), show session-level cost and end-to-end time-to-first-meaningful-response.
- Burst stress: short 30s microburst tests (1x->10x QPS), capture p95/p99 dynamics and error/retry behavior.

Experiment matrix (priority order):
1) Quick field bench (SE-friendly): 128-token single-turn p50/p95 comparison vs Competitor A, 50 QPS, 5-minute runs. Produce an SE deck slide with numbers and reproducible script. (Owner: Marco Li)
2) Session amortization sim: multi-turn 10x-turn sessions, 500 users simulated, compare session $/user. (Owner: Asha Nair + Bench team)
3) Microburst tail test: 1-minute ramps to 10x, repeat across 3 regions. Capture fallback events. (Owner: SRE + Bench team)
4) Price-normalized cost report: map observed GPU-time -> $ by cloud SKU, include sensitivity to reserved vs on-demand. (Owner: Finance liaison)

Key proof-point thresholds (for sales claims):
- Claim A (field): "~30% faster p95 on common LLM queries in-hosted API" — requires p95 delta >=25% in 2/3 model families.
- Claim B (cost): "15–35% lower per-token compute cost for chat workloads" — requires conservative median of normalized cost delta >=15% across session sim.
- Claim C (session): "Cut session compute by ~25% via caching + routing" — requires session-level cost reduction >=20% in multi-turn sims.

Competitive notes (quick sketches — confirm with PD/bench before public use):
- Competitor A: strong single-request latency on small models but limited prefix caching; pricing opaque for reserved/committed capacity; usually higher tail under bursts.
- Competitor B: emphasizes model catalog breadth and pre-built tools; less optimized batching on their multi-tenant endpoints.
- Competitor C: aggressive spot pricing but higher cold-starts and no built-in session cache; better if you accept eventual consistency on latency.

Sample elevator scripts (for AE / SE):
- Opening: "Most teams we talk to pay for a lot of repeated tokens across sessions — we reduce those costs natively with per-session caching and smarter routing, which means either a cheaper bill or richer UX for the same budget."
- Demo prompt: "Show me a 6-turn chat summarization where the model remembers earlier context; measure time to first useful response and cumulative tokens."
- Objection handling (pricing): "We provide a transparent mapping from GPU-hours to $/1k tokens in our benchmark report — if you have committed capacity we can model your exact bill and show the delta."

Customer-facing artifacts to produce (MVP list):
- 1-page sell sheet with 3 callouts: p95 delta, $/session savings, resilience claim + customer quote template.
- SE reproducible script (bash + python) to run 128-token p95 bench vs competitor endpoints.
- Public bench repo entry with sanitized configs and CI job that runs nightly smoke tests (owner: Bench GitHub)

Open questions / risks:
- Competitor endpoints: some have rate limits / protection that will bias comparisons — need SE sandbox accounts and opt-in A/B with customers.
- Pricing normalization: cloud spot discounts/reservations materially change $/1k token math — we need Finance inputs for conservative assumptions.
- Dataset realism: synthetic traffic is easier to reproduce but may not capture real user session drift — plan to run on 2 customer anonymized traces.

Next steps and owners (2-week cadence):
- Week 0–1: Marco to create SE quick-bench script + sample slide. Asha to draft sell-sheet copy.
- Week 1–2: Bench team runs full synthetic matrix and posts results to linked GitHub. SRE runs microburst tests in two regions.
- Week 2: PM/Finance review of $ mapping; iterate claims to conservative language.
- Week 3: Ship SE kit and public sell-sheet; schedule training for 3 field teams.

Notes-to-self (informal):
- Keep claims conservative; prefer "up to" and ranges backed by median+CI rather than single-run deltas.
- Capture raw logs for later root-cause if something looks off.
- Prioritize reproducibility over flashy numbers — field credibility matters.

References / starting scripts:
- bench repo: github:benchmarks/per-request-experiments#12 (see /scripts/quick_p95.sh)
- sample Confluence doc: GT-MKT/PerRequest-Econ-2025
- Jira epic: GTMECO-119

Unresolved wording suggestions for PMM:
- Avoid phrase "cheaper per token" in isolation — pair with "per-session" or "per-feature" framing to reflect workload differences.
- Use example customer anonymized numbers where possible e.g. "Customer X cut session compute by ~28% for their chat use case" (only include after customer permission).

-- end of brief --

(rough draft, feel free to carve into 1-pager + SE script checklist)
